title: Experts: What China wants from the COP31 climate talks - Carbon Brief
gist: Six China experts expect Beijing to prioritise defending multilateralism and attacking unilateral trade measures on clean tech at COP31 in Turkey, while resisting new finance or fossil-phase-out obligations. A key test is how China responds to the presidency's electrification initiative; skeptics note China's own renewables buildout slowed sharply in 2026 while coal construction continues.

insights.claim: Kate Logan of Asia Society Policy Institute expects China's top COP31 priority to be upholding multilateralism, and says China may be satisfied with a conference that produces no major drama and little else given constrained expectations.
insights.speaker: Kate Logan
insights.so_what: Low expectations for COP31 breakthroughs; limited market-moving outcomes.

insights.locator: In an era where global climate cooperation

insights.claim: China's environment vice-minister Li Gao called for upholding multilateralism, sending a 'clear political signal' of unity, and an 'open and efficient' trade system that facilitates clean-energy technology adoption.
insights.speaker: Li Gao
insights.so_what: Beijing's official COP31 line centres trade openness for its clean-tech exports.

insights.claim: Prof Ryna Cui notes there isn't much on the formal COP31 agenda; the focus on implementation and delivery suits China because of its domestic transition progress and the overseas opportunity to sell low-cost Chinese clean technologies.
insights.speaker: Ryna Cui
entities: University of Maryland Center for Global Sustainability
insights.so_what: Implementation framing aligns climate diplomacy with Chinese export interests.
insights.locator: There isn’t much on the formal negotiation

insights.claim: Experts expect China to use COP31 to oppose unilateral trade measures such as tariffs on its clean technologies, with an open question whether it pushes for a dedicated agenda item on trade, since COP30's trade outcomes mostly relegated discussion to mid-year technical meetings.
insights.speaker: Kate Logan
insights.so_what: Trade barriers on clean tech (e.g. EU CBAM, tariffs) will be contested in UN climate forums.
insights.locator: Nevertheless, expect China’s vision for multilateralism

insights.claim: Greenpeace East Asia's Yao Zhe says China's new five-year plan on climate action calls for proper handling of climate-trade issues and the free flow of low-carbon products, and expects a continued push to integrate trade perspectives into negotiations.
insights.speaker: Yao Zhe
insights.so_what: Trade-climate linkage is now formal Chinese strategy.
insights.locator: At COP31, I expect a continued push

insights.claim: Dr Joseph Dellatte of Institut Montaigne will watch whether China keeps framing the transition around access to Chinese technologies and open markets, or shows willingness to share industrial benefits via local manufacturing, joint ventures and technology sharing.
insights.speaker: Joseph Dellatte
insights.so_what: Localisation/JV concessions would signal a shift in China's clean-tech export model.

insights.claim: Yao Zhe argues Beijing increasingly views climate diplomacy as clean-energy diplomacy leveraging its strength in renewables, EVs, batteries and grids, and should welcome a global electrification initiative but remain reluctant to link it to transitioning away from fossil fuels.
insights.speaker: Yao Zhe
insights.so_what: Expect China to back electrification targets but resist fossil phase-out language.
insights.quote: it likely remains reluctant to link these targets to any commitments regarding transitioning away from fossil fuels
insights.locator: I will also be watching how China responds

insights.claim: Ryna Cui suggests that as China reaches its coal and oil peak, it may gain space to lead the global 'transitioning away from fossil fuels' agenda, more likely via bilateral and multilateral engagement than formal negotiations.
insights.speaker: Ryna Cui
insights.so_what: Chinese demand peaks could eventually shift its diplomatic stance on fossil phase-out.
insights.quote: as China reaches its coal and oil peak, it may open up space for increased interests and leadership in the global “transitioning away from fossil fuels” agenda
insights.locator: One thing exciting for me to watch

insights.claim: Cui adds that China can contribute to rapid abatement of methane, industrial nitrous oxide, HFCs and other non-CO2 gases as part of its 2035 all-sector, all-greenhouse gas NDC.
insights.speaker: Ryna Cui
insights.so_what: Non-CO2 abatement is a near-term area for Chinese climate action.

insights.claim: After disclosing at COP29 that it had provided and mobilised over 177bn yuan ($26.5bn) in climate finance for developing countries since 2016, China has refrained from further quantitative updates while insisting developed countries lead on finance.
insights.speaker: Kate Logan
insights.so_what: China avoids being drawn into contributor obligations under the $300bn goal.

insights.claim: Kate Logan expects China to let other developing countries push the finance agenda while acting as an end-game broker to protect its own interests, amid anxiety about added pressure following US withdrawal.
insights.speaker: Kate Logan
insights.so_what: China likely to stay a finance recipient-side voice rather than contributor.
insights.quote: China may be happy to let other developing countries push this agenda while serving as a broker in the end game to ensure its own interests are protected.

insights.claim: Ma Jun of the Institute of Public and Environmental Affairs says overshooting 1.5C is almost unavoidable and expects China to seek clearer climate finance delivery, especially for adaptation, alongside methane cuts and just-transition support.
insights.speaker: Ma Jun
entities: Institute of Public and Environmental Affairs
insights.so_what: Adaptation finance is likely the focal finance ask.
insights.quote: With the risk of overshooting 1.5C almost unavoidable

insights.claim: Johns Hopkins SAIS professor Jeremy Wallace argues China seems more interested in fighting 'unfair' tariffs abroad than accelerating green-tech adoption at home, noting its renewables buildout slowed dramatically in 2026 while new coal power and coal chemical facilities continue to be built.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Wallace
insights.so_what: China's domestic slowdown weakens its leadership claim and may intensify export pressure.
insights.quote: China’s renewables buildout has slowed dramatically in 2026, while new coal power and coal chemical facilities continue to be built.

insights.claim: Wallace says the Chinese government has restricted firms from taking their best manufacturing innovations abroad when building overseas factories.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Wallace
insights.so_what: Limits technology transfer from Chinese overseas factories; relevant to localisation strategies of importing countries.
insights.quote: The Chinese government has restricted firms from taking their best manufacturing innovations out of the country when building factories abroad.

insights.claim: Dellatte will watch whether Beijing supports commitments linking electrification to cleaner grids and uses its influence to bring reluctant fossil-fuel producers on board, as a test of accepting greater responsibility while leading developing countries.
insights.speaker: Joseph Dellatte
insights.so_what: Signals at COP31 on grid decarbonisation would mark a real ambition shift.
